item.title: Draft law urges strict anti-graft compliance
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03
Chinese enterprises operating across borders are expected to face more regulated management, with a draft law requiring them to establish integrity departments or appoint dedicated staff — based on their size, business scope and risk prevention and control — for clean governance and compliance. The draft law on combating cross-border corruption was submitted for its second reading on Monday to the ongoing session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, China's top legislature. The session runs through Friday. The document was first submitted for deliberation in late August. According to the latest version of the draft, which is divided into six chapters and 47 articles, relevant companies may formulate separate clean compliance rules for their overseas departments or subsidiaries, assign dedicated officers to these units in light of actual circumstances, and formulate duty guidelines for them. Yang Chao, an associate professor of law at Beijing Normal University, noted that corporate clean compliance is a key pillar for enterprises to meet their anti-corruption obligations. Welcoming the provisions on clean compliance in the draft law, Yang said that such measures "will help prevent improper benefits from being channeled through intermediaries and will also help push companies to integrate anti-corruption work into their day-to-day management and operations". "Beyond that, legislating on these matters will provide institutional safeguards for enterprises going global and for jointly building a road of integrity with other countries," she added. Zhang Lei, a law professor at Beijing Normal University, said the provisions in the draft law indicate that the management of Chinese enterprises expanding overseas or engaging in international operations will become more standardized. Setting up integrity departments or appointing dedicated staff will further promote the fulfillment of clean compliance obligations by such enterprises, and will also help guide enterprises to operate lawfully, reducing — or even eliminating — the occurrence of cross-border corruption from within, he said. Zhang noted that tackling cross-border corruption through legislation is a crucial demonstration of full and rigorous Party self-governance, which was underscored in a resolution adopted at the fifth plenary session of the 20th Communist Party of China Central Committee that concluded on Thursday. "The resolution emphasizes the need to enhance international cooperation in the fight against corruption, intensify efforts to track down fugitives and recover illicit assets, and improve the effectiveness and efficiency of managing cross-border cases. These priorities are also underscored in the draft law," he said. Zhang also highlighted that the formulation of the law represents a significant step in the path of anti-corruption with Chinese characteristics. "It serves as an important window for showcasing to the international community China's achievements in combating corruption through the rule of law," he said. While outlining requirements for enterprises, the draft law places greater emphasis on respecting human rights and adds provisions that strengthen the protection of state secrets, business and trade secrets, as well as personal data and privacy. Official data shows that China is a major trading partner for more than 160 countries and regions, and its total trade in goods has ranked first in the world for nine consecutive years. By the end of 2025, Chinese investors had established more than 50,000 overseas enterprises across 190 countries and regions. caoyin@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Swap facility gives boost to A shares
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03
China's financial regulators are stepping up efforts to bolster capital market liquidity and stability, with the central bank preparing a fresh round of funding support for institutional investors and the securities regulator moving to encourage more share buybacks and attract additional long-term capital. The People's Bank of China announced on Monday that it would conduct a new round of operations under its securities, funds and insurance companies swap facility (SFISF) on Tuesday to support the sound and stable development of the capital market. The move will have a one-year tenor, with possible extensions, the PBOC said in a statement. So far, 31 securities and fund management firms have applied for more than 100 billion yuan ($15 billion) under the operation. Introduced in 2024, the facility allows eligible securities firms, fund managers and insurers to swap assets including bonds, stock exchange-traded funds and CSI 300 Index constituent shares for highly liquid assets such as government bonds and central bank bills. The funds obtained should be used exclusively for capital market investments, including stock and stock ETF investments and market-making. Lou Feipeng, a researcher at Postal Savings Bank of China, said the new SFISF operation will provide nonbanking financial institutions with liquidity support that can help break the vicious cycle of redemptions and forced sell-offs, facilitating countercyclical share purchases during market downturns without expanding the monetary base. In the short term, the facility can channel fresh capital into the stock market and improve investor risk appetite, while over the medium term, it can reduce market vulnerabilities and mitigate forced selling, Lou said. The move comes as the China Securities Regulatory Commission is also considering a package of measures to strengthen the market's resilience and bolster investor expectations, including making it easier for listed companies to conduct market-stabilizing buybacks, which are aimed at stabilizing their market values and protecting shareholder interests. The proposed changes include adding shares trading below their initial public offering prices as a trigger for market-stabilizing buybacks, easing relevant trading restrictions and requiring newly listed companies to honor their market-stabilizing buyback commitments. Before the revised rules take effect, the CSRC will encourage eligible companies — particularly major index constituents and leading tech firms — to actively conduct share buybacks, the commission said on Monday. During the first 10 months of the year, 645 Shanghai- and Shenzhen-listed firms announced 237.7 billion yuan in buyback plans, while 747 companies executed repurchases totaling 134.5 billion yuan, both setting record highs, official data showed. The A-share market rebounded on Monday in anticipation of supportive measures, with media reports during the weekend speculating that two central State-owned enterprises — China Reform Holdings and China Chengtong Holdings — would obtain additional loans for shareholding increases and buybacks. On Monday, the CSI 300 Index closed up 0.79 percent at 4016.92 points while the tech-heavy STAR 50 Index jumped as much as 3.11 percent. Yang Delong, chief economist at First Seafront Fund, said policymakers are making all-out efforts to support the capital market. A recent surge in ETF trading volume suggests that major institutional investors may have begun stepping up purchases to support a rebound in asset prices. Yang said the recent sell-off in artificial intelligence-related tech shares largely reflects a correction of previously overzealous transactions, with forced liquidations and panic selling exacerbating the declines. Many leading AI tech shares may now be undervalued, creating room for a valuation recovery that could become a key driver of a market rebound. zhoulanxv@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Ancient walnut-rolling pastime finds new admirers
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03
When Italian content creator Carolina Di Condio first met her future husband, who is Chinese, in Milan eight years ago, she noticed something unusual. He was constantly rolling two walnuts around in his palm. Fascinated by the movement and the clicking sound, she tried it herself, only to discover it was not as easy as it looked. But one question kept bothering her. "Can I just crack them open and eat them?" she finally asked. Her husband's expression was unforgettable — somewhere between amusement and horror. That was Di Condio's introduction to wenwan walnuts — literally "plaything walnuts" — which are not meant to be eaten but specially cultivated and selected for handling in a centuries-old Chinese pastime, in which people roll the walnuts in their palms, gradually polishing the shells to create treasured personal possessions. Years later, a Dior invitation featuring a pair of wenwan walnuts caught her attention. Drawing on her background in fashion, Di Condio saw the connection between the Chinese tradition and luxury craftsmanship. "Just as the walnuts gradually develop their own patina over years of polishing and care, I believe that the value of beautiful things often lies in the time, craftsmanship and attention invested in them," Di Condio said. For some collectors in China, the investment begins long before the walnuts are actually bought by wenwan enthusiasts. Wang Hongduo, 36, a walnut dealer in Laishui county, Hebei province, knows this firsthand. About five years ago, Wang, who specializes in rare wenwan walnuts, acquired an unusual specimen with nine distinct ridges. "A good walnut should have a well-balanced shape and evenly arranged ridges. To make a pair, the two walnuts must also closely resemble each other," he said. In September 2025, a matching nine-ridged walnut surfaced through another dealer, and Wang was finally able to complete the pair. His patience paid off at a local competition on Oct 16 this year, where the pair won the top award in the unusual shape category. Wang later turned down an offer of 450,000 yuan ($67,670) for the unique pair. The offer price was exceptional, but for those who want to give the pastime a try, a pair can cost just tens or hundreds of yuan. The appeal of wenwan walnuts as collectibles is not new. The tradition flourished during the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1644-1911) dynasties, when scholars and wealthy collectors prized them for their distinctive shapes, intricate patterns and the glossy patina they developed over time. Today, Laishui is one of China's major production centers of wenwan walnuts. More than 80,000 farming households benefit from the industry, which generates over 2.2 billion yuan annually, according to local authorities. Wider reach The customers walking into shops like Wang's are not necessarily older collectors traditionally associated with the pastime. Wang estimates that more than 90 percent of buyers in his high-end specialty walnut business were born in the 1990s or 2000s. Among the younger enthusiasts is Song Yuxuan, 26, who works in the finance industry and has been collecting wenwan walnuts for four years. His interest began with a chance encounter in a park, where he spotted elderly men rolling walnuts in their palms. Curious, he went home and practiced with ordinary edible walnuts for two or three months before purchasing a proper pair. It was at a time when Song had just begun working. "When I first started working, I hardly knew anyone. I took up wenwan walnuts around that time and found it helped me relax whenever work got stressful," he said. What began as a small hobby is now a part of his daily routine. He owns 20 to 30 pairs and sometimes visits Wang and other dealers to meet fellow enthusiasts, exchange experiences and look for new additions to his collection. But the pleasure is not simply in acquiring more walnuts. "I think some young people enjoy watching the walnuts change color, from their original pale appearance to a deep reddish shade. Seeing that transformation gives you a sense of achievement," he said. Song has also introduced the pastime to his girlfriend, who now enjoys using a pair of her own. The fascination has also spread beyond China. Videos of people playing with Chinese walnuts have attracted millions of views on TikTok and Instagram, introducing the unfamiliar tradition to viewers around the world. Di Condio, the Italian content creator, occasionally rolls her husband's wenwan walnuts, although she jokes that she needs a pair of hazelnuts instead, because her hands are smaller. What resonates with her is the connection to the Italian idea of la dolce vita, which celebrates life's simple pleasures. In an age of constant phone notifications and endless to-do lists, she believes the pastime offers an alternative to the rush of modern life. "They invite us to slow down and enjoy a moment without having to achieve anything," she said.

item.title: China's affluent population on the rise
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03
Despite uncertainties and headwinds in the global market, the growing ranks of China's affluent remain financially confident and active, though their engagement in long-term planning is still far from adequate, according to a recent industry report. The China Rising Affluent Financial Well-Being Index, which marks its 10th consecutive edition this year with the latest one released on Oct 27, registered the largest year-on-year increase since 2021 — 71.99 — up 1.64 from a year earlier. According to experts from Shanghai Jiao Tong University's Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance (SAIF) and global financial services provider Charles Schwab — the compilers of the index — this is driven by positive developments across all four measured dimensions, namely, investor confidence, planning, wealth management and engagement in financial services. The Chinese rising affluent group — individuals with an average personal annual income of 125,000 to 1 million yuan ($18,800 to 150,400) and investable assets of less than $1 million — has shown rising financial confidence ever since the index was first rolled out in 2017. Closer scrutiny of this group is crucial, as they will become a major force reshaping the Chinese financial sector with their rising affluence and increasingly urgent demand for wealth management services, said Thomas Pixley, general manager of Charles Schwab (Shanghai). Reasons for such optimism have changed over the past three years, evolving from stable household income and expected increases in property prices, to recovery in financial markets and people's rising confidence in their wealth management capabilities. However, planning is inadequate among China's rising affluent group. Though the planning sub-index has slightly ticked up to 36.21 from a year earlier, the reading is still around a historic low level. Only 54.9 percent of the 4,588 interviewees have established financial plans, 20 percent lower than that a decade ago. Most respondents simply equate financial targets with 10 percent annual increase in their assets. Few have come up with systematic planning regarding retirement or children's education. "To some, planning is unnecessary as they have stable incomes at present or are content with their current financial status. Others think current financial planning may not apply to future scenarios once major changes take place. All these are based on the false assumption that financial planning is static. But the fact is, financial planning is a dynamic process which requires regular revision," said Wu Fei, an SAIF professor. A complicated scenario can be seen in the perception and actual behaviors regarding asset management. The rising affluent population's self-perceived risk profiles have become increasingly polarized. Compared with 2017, the share of respondents identifying as conservative and aggressive investors increased by 52.2 percent and 45 percent, respectively. But cash and fixed-term deposits take up nearly half of their asset management total. Low-risk assets take up about 70 percent of all their portfolios if banks' wealth management products are included. The ratio of cash and fixed-term deposits even take up 44.5 percent of assets of self-perceived aggressive investors, far exceeding mainstream global industry expectations. While interest in properties — the core asset of Chinese households in the past — has been declining, financial products have not immediately caught up to fill in the gap, said Wu. "This points to the transition in the Chinese financial sector when professional investment advisory institutions should step in and seek substantial development," he added. Lisa Hunt, managing director for Charles Schwab, suggested that mutual fund products can be given a bigger play in China. Inherently diversified, these products can lead to higher asset management activity in both passive and active investing styles, Hunt said. Chen Peng, chairman of investment services provider Morningstar in China, said the size and coverage of long-term capital — such as pension funds — should be expanded. Its proportion directed to the capital market should also be increased, which is conducive to the performance of quality companies and investors' interests, Chen said. shijing@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: From surviving to thriving
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03
From surviving to thriving Rare-disease patients seek improved quality of life amid medical advances Ten years ago patients with rare diseases would phone Wang Yiou's support organization in despair, many complaining they had no medication or were unable to afford treatment. Today the situation is markedly different thanks in no small way to proactive government policies and the country's advances in innovative drug treatment. The topics brought up in phone calls today have become increasingly diverse, said Wang, founder and secretary-general of the Illness Challenge Foundation, a Beijing-based organization that provides support to rare-disease patients across the country. For example, parents who take care of their sick children worry about sudden seizures at night and are unable to sleep through the night, hoping for monitoring methods. At school, children forget to take their medication and need inconspicuous smart pillboxes that don't cause psychological pressure, she cited as another example. "Over the past decade, many rare-disease patients in China have moved from seeking medical treatment everywhere and having no available drugs to a new stage today, hoping for more convenient travel and socializing as well as better social integration and expression," she said. "Many people's life conditions are very different from 10 years ago," said Wang, who has osteogenesis imperfecta, commonly known as brittle bone disease. In mid-October, the foundation hosted an event in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, a hub for tech firms. Ten teams, including school students and young workers, showcased their solutions to the daily needs of rare-disease patients to help them live more comfortably. Despite all the improvements, there is still a long way to go in the treatment of rare diseases, experts said. There are over 10,000 known rare diseases worldwide, and about 20 million people in China are affected. Globally, less than 10 percent of rare diseases have available treatments. In China, about 60 percent of patients with treatable diseases can access medication.

item.title: Protection, coordination to make Yellow River more beautiful
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03
President Xi Jinping has called for sustained efforts to strengthen coordinated protection and governance of the Yellow River, making the nation's mother river more beautiful and ensuring that it benefits the Chinese nation for generations to come. In a recent instruction, Xi, who is also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, said that 80 years of Party-led efforts to harness the river had fundamentally changed its history of frequent levee breaches and created a miracle of flood safety year after year. These achievements fully demonstrate the significant strengths of the socialist system, he said. He called for adherence to a water management approach that prioritizes water conservation, balances spatial distribution, undertakes systematic approaches and gives full play to the roles of both the government and the market. Efforts should be made to further improve the framework of holistic protection and collaboration, advance ecological conservation and high-quality development in the Yellow River Basin, and strengthen the national ecological security barrier, Xi said. He also emphasized ensuring the river's long-term stability and carrying forward the Yellow River culture. Xi's instruction was conveyed on Monday at a work conference on comprehensively advancing the protection and governance of the Yellow River in Zhengzhou, Henan province, which Vice-Premier Liu Guozhong attended and addressed. The 5,464-kilometer Yellow River flows through nine provinces and autonomous regions before meeting the Bohai Sea. Its basin supports about 12 percent of China's population and accounts for about 14 percent of the country's GDP. Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, Xi has inspected all nine provinces and autonomous regions along the Yellow River and chaired three symposiums on the ecological conservation and high-quality development of the basin. zhaojia@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Joint Mideast peace efforts urged
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02
The Middle East and the Gulf region should not become a wrestling arena for major-country rivalry or geopolitical conflicts, President Xi Jinping said on Monday, reiterating China's commitment to working with Arab states and countries of the Gulf Cooperation Council to strive for lasting peace in the region. Xi made the remarks during talks with Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik Al Said of Oman, who was on a state visit to China from Sunday to Monday. This was the first visit to China by an Omani head of state since the two countries established diplomatic ties 48 years ago. Xi said that concerted efforts are needed by all parties to foster and safeguard peace and stability in the Middle East and the Gulf region. China has consistently been committed to ending hostility and promoting peace in the Middle East, and hopes to contribute wisdom and solutions to resolving the region's security dilemmas, he said. The nation will continue to advocate resolving disputes through political and diplomatic means and will support countries in the region in building a common homeland of good neighborliness, development, security and cooperation, Xi added. He expressed China's willingness to strengthen communication and coordination with Oman and other Arab and Gulf Cooperation Council countries to work together toward restoring peace and tranquility in the region and achieving lasting security and stability. The Omani sultan said that China plays an indispensable leading role in maintaining world peace and stability. Oman highly appreciates China's just stance on the Middle East issue and is willing to closely coordinate with China to uphold international law, advocate for the peaceful resolution of disputes, and jointly promote regional and global security and stability, he said. In a joint statement released on Monday on deepening the China-Oman strategic partnership, both countries expressed their encouragement for the United States and Iran to adhere to peaceful options, achieve a comprehensive ceasefire and cessation of hostilities as early as possible, and resume dialogue and negotiations to reach a comprehensive agreement that includes the nuclear issue. Both countries also maintain that the situation in the Strait of Hormuz should return to normal and safe navigation is restored, the statement said, and they agree to maintain communication on issues related to the strait. China has played a positive role on the Middle East issue. While meeting with Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, in Beijing in April, Xi put forward a four-point proposal on promoting peace and stability in the Middle East. He called for adhering to the principle of peaceful coexistence, the principle of national sovereignty, the principle of international rule of law, and a coordinated approach to development and security. On Monday, Foreign Minister Wang Yi met in Beijing with Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, emphasizing that dialogue and negotiation are the only viable solutions to the ongoing Middle East conflict. All parties should seek political resolution of the conflict in a rational and pragmatic spirit, rather than resorting to military confrontation, Wang said, adding that China will continue to work with all parties to restore peace in the region. Speaking at a regular news conference on Monday, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said that China will send its special envoy to the Middle East to visit Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia this month to implement the series of initiatives and proposals put forward by Xi on the Middle East issue. The visit aims to facilitate peace talks and ease tensions, and play a constructive role in maintaining regional peace and stability, she said. Bilateral cooperation During Monday's talks, the two heads of state pledged to promote bilateral ties. They witnessed the signing of multiple cooperation documents in areas such as Beidou Navigation Satellite System application, industrial and supply chains, green development, local currency swaps, digital payments and digital currency. Xi said that Sultan Haitham's visit will become an important chapter in the history of China-Oman relations, injecting strong momentum into the development of bilateral ties. He said that expanding and deepening China-Oman relations is a strategic choice for both sides, follows the trend of the times and historical development, and meets the common aspirations of the two peoples. China is committed to promoting high-quality development and expanding high-standard opening-up, which will bring greater opportunities to Oman and other countries worldwide, Xi said. He expressed China's willingness to deepen the synergy of development strategies with Oman and be a stable and reliable partner in the energy sector, a partner with promising potential in investment, and a partner in fostering innovation within advanced technologies. Sultan Haitham said that under the strong leadership of President Xi, China has become a major political and economic country in the world, making significant contributions to global prosperity and stability. Oman firmly adheres to the one-China principle and supports China in safeguarding its national sovereignty and territorial integrity, he said. He expressed hope to take this visit as a new starting point to explore more cooperation opportunities and build a future-oriented partnership. caodesheng@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Yan An in Yan'an: Rediscovering the spirit of Nanniwan
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02
"Who wouldn't want a tractor of their own?" This unexpected remark from China Daily reporter Yan An may leave you wondering. As the 90th anniversary of the Long March (1934-36) is marked this year, Yan An returns to Yan'an, the final destination of the Long March and a city whose name shares the pronunciation of her own, to explore how the spirit of the Long March continues to inspire young people today. This time, she revisits Nanniwan, once hailed as the "Jiangnan of northern Shaanxi". Today, Nanniwan is not only taking on a new look but is also being transformed by a new generation of farmers. Meet Ma Qiang, a Party member born in the 1990s who returned to his hometown to start an agricultural business. With modern farming machinery, he helps local villagers work more efficiently, boost agricultural output and increase their incomes through the farmers' cooperative. Join Yan An in the cradle of the Chinese revolution and discover how modernization is bringing new life to this historic land.

item.title: Portugal-China chamber official on China's success
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02
Bernardo Mendia, secretary-general of the Portugal-China Chamber of Commerce and Industry, recently told China Daily's Global Lens that long-term planning, and a governance system that promotes officials based on proven performance are key to China's development. Long-term planning, he said, underpins stability and predictability — for investors and for the country itself. He called long-term planning China's "secret sauce" — the factor that has taken China from 1978 to becoming the world's second-largest economy. He added that a stable China with a long-term vision is injecting stability into an unstable world. (Reporter: Luan Ruiying, Video: Pan Yixuan, Intern: Gao Jiayi)
